course_description:
You will undertake original research and produce a publicly accessible digital media product that may examine a significant political, social or cultural issue.

Digital media technologies are rapidly reshaping every aspect of our lives. But what could they look like in the future? How might digital media technologies continue to transform, and how will they, in turn, transform us?

Digital Project is a course that combines media theory with audiovisual media making skills. In the course, you will use the process of designing and creating digital media artefacts to critically reflect on the world around you, and to imagine future possibilities of media. This course asks the questions: What is digital media? By what social, technical, industrial and cultural forces is it shaped? What might digital media become?

Across the semester, you will develop a “digital project” centred around your own original idea for a speculative digital media technology of the future that will change the world. You will complete a design proposal and a portfolio of digital media artefacts, requiring you to synthesise knowledgeﾠ and connect theory with practice, bringing together theoretical frameworks and technical skills. This course will teach you how to think creatively and critically, and how to translate your thinking into audiovisual media assets and products.

Please note: Familiarity with the Adobe suite is a requirement of this course. Activities in classes will help you refresh these skills, so please note that you must bring your devices (with Adobe software installed) to workshops each week to participate in the activities.

course_aims: The course aims to understand and addressﾠhow media technologies and platforms are culturally and historically situated through upper level media theory, theory-centred readings,ﾠand reflective, research methodologies in online and tutorial sessionsﾠthat develop creative, flexible thinking and include both individual and peer-assisted modes of learning.ﾠAssessments are designed around a semester-long project that connects upper level media theory toﾠthe project of conceiving a new media technology.

assessment_details.title: In-Class Activities
assessment_details.task_description: In this course, workshops are designed to support your learning and actively scaffold assessment tasks. Eight (8) workshops will include a set of in-class activities relating to the weekly topic, reading and lecture, and will involve reflective writing, responding to questions about course content, and practical making tasks to be completed in the workshop (requiring the use of Adobe software). These tasks will require critical thinking and prior preparation through attending lectures and engaging with course readings and resources. These activities and responses, unless necessarily different due to the nature of the task, will be handwritten and the use of machine translation will not be permitted. They are worth 5 marks each, with a total of 30 marks available. The best 6 workshops of the 8 available workshops will be counted towards your grade. Because only 6 of the 8 count, the assessment already builds in the flexibility to miss up to 2 sessions — for illness or any other reason — with no penalty and no documentation required. These must be completed in class. There are no opportunities to re-take an individual exercise, and no alternative assessment is available except in the specific circumstances set out below. As this is an internal course, you must make yourself available to complete each exercise at the scheduled date, time and venue. Unless otherwise directed, these are handwritten, closed-book tasks: no written material, electronic material or electronic devices may be used. All such items must remain in your bag or under your desk, and all electronic devices must be switched off or in airplane mode. If a device emits any noise, you may be subject to an allegation of misconduct and the item may be confiscated for the duration of the exercise. You may bring suitable writing implements (in a clear container), water in a clear bottle with the label removed, and disposable earplugs. Alternative assessment and accommodations If you have a Student Access Plan relevant to this task, please contact the course coordinator as early as possible. Reasonable accommodations can be made for matters documented in a Student Access Plan (for example, if you are unable to handwrite under timed conditions). The 2-session buffer described above is intended to cover ordinary absences. A separate make-up session is available only to students who, for a genuine and documented reason, miss more than 2 of the exercises — for example, a sudden or serious illness, or another documented cause requiring a lengthy absence. Missing 2 or fewer sessions is already covered by the best-6-of-8 structure and does not qualify for a make-up. To be considered for a make-up session or any other alternative arrangement, you must contact the course coordinator with your documentation as soon as possible after the circumstances arise. assessment_details.title: Media Proposal and Design Draft
assessment_details.task_description: How do digital media technologies shape society? How are they in turn shaped by society? For the Media Proposal and Design Draft, you will propose a speculative media technology that will allow you to explore these driving questions. You will research, conceptualise and design a speculative media technology or platform that is plausible as a digital media technology of the near future. The idea and design of the media technology should respond to a social, political or cultural issue, and must be informed by independent academic research and relevant course material. You will submit 1) a design rationale of 1000 words explaining the features of your design, your design process, and how your design relates to a social, political or cultural issue. You will also create 2) an audiovisual media product demonstrating the features of your design, such as diagrams or product mockups, alongside a process walkthrough. Further details will be made available in a task sheet and rubric on Blackboard. Any use of generative AI must be acknowledged and explained, and you must show evidence of having created assets WITHOUT the use of generative AI to fulfil the criteria. assessment_details.title: Media Portfolio and Consultation
assessment_details.due_date: 30/10/2026 4:00 pm Consultations will take place in workshops in Week 11 and 12.
assessment_details.task_description: To explore your speculative media technology from the Media Proposal and Design Draft, you will create a series of digital media artefacts (photos, advertisements, videos, social media content, packaging designs etc.) about the media technology you created for the media proposal. You will also present a reflection (1000 words) explaining the context and design of the artefacts. These artefacts should be chosen to demonstrate how the media technology you created for the first assessment was marketed and received by society, exploring the consequences of the technology through social, political and cultural lenses. Your own creation of assets (photos, drawings, raw video etc) will be highly valued. As with the Media Proposal and Design Draft, your Media Portfolio must address the course driving questions: How do digital media technologies shape society? How are they in turn shaped by society? The final assessment consists of four components: Media Portfolio Critical Reflection Process Walkthrough Consultation (in person) Media Portfolio: Students are expected to hand in a media portfolio that builds on their designs from the Media Proposal and Design Draft. The portfolio should explore social, cultural or political issues through audio-visual means, bringing strong understandings of media theory to life. The content of the portfolio should be discussed with your tutor in advance of submission, but must have been created using the Adobe suite unless permission is received from your tutor. It can include a wide variety of mediums and forms, but all media must be edited and polished with attention to typography and other design aspects, and incorporating strong prose or copy. If internet-sourced imagery is used, it has been cited and substantially altered in software programs alongside original material. The project should not rely on AI produced imagery in a way that jeopardises the project's originality and the student's demonstration of advanced media production skills. Critical Reflection: You will write 1000 words from your own perspective that explains how the portfolio answers the driving question of the unit. How does the portfolio use design to speculate about the future and critically speak to the present? You must do this with reference to course readings and materials and your own academic research. This should be submitted alongside the portfolio. You must also respond to feedback from your tutor in the consultation. Process Walkthrough : You must submit a document explaining your creative process, documenting how you made the media artefacts you have included in your portfolio. You must clearly document your step by step process with screenshots, detailing the software you have used to create the artefacts and the technical skills you have demonstrated in doing so. Consultation: You will be assigned a week (last two weeks of workshops) to attend a short consultation with your tutor about your project. You will be asked questions by your tutor that may ask you to explain the media technology, the media artefacts you've created, and how they speak to a social, political or cultural issue with reference to academic research and course materials. You will be given verbal feedback from your tutor to incorporate into your final portfolio submission. Attending the consultation is a hurdle requirement to pass this assessment item and is thus mandatory. If you are ill on your scheduled consultation day you must contact staff before the scheduled workshop and will need to arrange a medical certificate. Further details will be made available in a task sheet and rubric on Blackboard. Any use of generative AI must be acknowledged and explained, and you must show evidence of having created assets WITHOUT the use of generative AI to fulfil the criteria. As the consultations are secure, there is no allowed generative AI during the consultation, and you will need to demonstrate your comprehension of your portfolio without the assistance of generative AI. Recording of Oral and Practical Assessment: All consultations will be recorded for marking purposes via recording facilities available where the assessment takes place (eg. ECHO360, Zoom, camera device) Recordings will be retained by the School of Communication and Arts for at least 12 months from the release of the final grade for the course. Recordings will be stored in a secure manner and will only be accessed by authorised school staff for the purposes of: Moderation of marking; Provision of feedback to the student(s) recorded; and/or Re-marking following a successful re-mark application Read full task description Hide full task description

policies_and_procedures: University policies and procedures apply to all aspects of student life. As a UQ student, you must comply with University-wide and program-specific requirements, including the: Student Code of Conduct Policy Student Integrity and Misconduct Policy and Procedure Assessment Procedure Examinations Procedure Reasonable Adjustments for Students Policy and Procedure AI for Assessment Guide Recording of Teaching Policy and Procedure Learn more about UQ policies on my.UQ and the Policy and Procedure Library . Course guidelines Communication Expectations While you are a student at UQ, all communication must be conducted according to the UQ Student Code of Conduct . The UQ Library has a helpful Communicate and collaborate online module . Email is the primary way for you to send messages to, and receive information from, the School and our staff. You must use your UQ email address (not a private address) to communicate with staff. You should add a clear subject line, including course code, and a 2-3 word statement. You can send email at any time, however, please do not expect responses outside normal working hours (Monday to Friday from ~8am to ~5pm). Emails that constitute bullying, harassment or discrimination against staff contravene the Student Code of Conduct. Emails like this will be reported to the University, and the matter will be pursued as misconduct. Learning activities
